source_text: The stainless steels evaluated in this study were prepared from commercially pure grades of Fe, Ni, ferrochrome, Mn, Mo, Si, manganese or chromium nitride, and chromium carbide. Melting was done in a vacuum induction furnace.The melting procedure consisted of: (1) melting Fe, Ni, Mo, Mn, and ferrochrome in a vacuum; (2) bleeding nitrogen into the furnace; and (3) introducing Mn4N or CrN, wrapped in iron foil, into the melt, as needed. After casting, only solid sections of the ingots were taken to prepare test specimens. The sections were first soaked for 30 minutes and hot rolled. The temperatures were 1205 C and 1095 C, depending upon hot ductility of the heats. The hot rolled specimens were pickled in a solution containing 10% HNO3 and 2% HF at 65 C to remove the hot working scale, cold rolled to 2 mm, annealed at 1065 C for 5 minutes, water quenched, and pickled again in the same HNO3-HF solution at 65 C. A small section was cut from each heat and used for chemical analysis.
notes: The initial soaking/rolling temperature had alternatives, so no temperature was assigned to that stage. Pickling solutions and temperatures were not used as test conditions.

source_text: Nitrogen, which is an austenite stabilizer, shifts the a-'y phase boundaries in Fe-Cr-Ni alloys, as described in Figure 8.
notes: General discussion of nitrogen and phase boundaries was not an observation of the sample.

source_text: The ingots were homogenized in A or He, usually at 1050-1100 oC for several hours. Ingots of Ni-Cr, Ni-Mo, and Cr-Fe were cold rolled to 0.25 cm, then annealed at 1000-1050 oC and water quenched. The Cr-Fe alloys containing more than 40% Cr were difficult to roll or swage, hence electrodes were machined directly from the homogenized ingot. Ingots of the lower % Cr-Fe alloys and of the stainless steels were swaged to about 0.45 cm diam rods, annealed at 1050 oC and water quenched. All electrodes measured approximately 2 cm long and were either 0.4 cm diam or 0.5 cm wide by 0.2 cm thick.
notes: Ranges and several hours were not reduced to point values. Subsequent annealing depended on alloy subgroup and was not assigned without row-specific evidence.

source_text: Two sets of laboratory-prepared ferritic alloys and two commercial ferritic stainless steels (Types 430 and 4341) were investigated. The high-purity 17% chromium, 17% Cr-l% Mo, and 17% Cr-3% Mo laboratory alloys were prepared by melting and casting in vacuum. The resulting ingots were hot-rolled to 0.64-cmthick sheet, which was cold-rolled to a 0.32-cm thickness, annealed for 1 hr at 815~ and water-quenched. The 18% Cr-2% Mo alloys modified by titanium and Type 434 is the proposed designation for stainless steel conraining 17% chromium and 1% molybdenum. nickel additions were produced by induction melting in an argon atmosphere, using the split-heat technique. In this technique, the base composition is melted, and part of the melt is poured off to produce an ingot; then to the balance of the melt, the required alloying additions are made and the next ingot is cast. This process is repeated until a series of the desired compositions is cast. The 18% Cr-2% Mo ingots were hotforged, hot-rolled to 0.76-cm-thick strips, and coldrolled to 0.38-cm-thick strips. The 18% Cr-2% Mo alloys containing titanium were annealed for 1 hr at 104O~ the minimum temperature that prevented formation of a second phase in the high titanium alloy, and then water-quenched. The rest of the 18% Cr-2% Mo materials and the hot-rolled, commercial Types 430 and 434 steels were annealed at 815~ for 1 hr and water-quenched.
notes: Different alloy subgroups received different annealing temperatures; the common time and cooling were retained, and temperature remained missing.

source_text: All surfaces of the cast slabs were ground to remove imperfections and provide good rolling surfaces before annealing 16 hours at 1200C in argon atmosphere. The slabs were hot rolled at 1090C to 1/16 inch thickness. Oxide scale was subsequently removed by sand blasting before a final annealing treatment. Following preparation, each alloy was hot rolled to 0.1 inch sheet and water quenched. Hot rolling temperatures were restricted to a maximum of 982C and a minimum of 816C. The hot rolled sheet was electropolished in an aqueous 15wt% NaCl/ 30wt%H2SO4 electrolyte to remove surface scale and sheared into 1 inch wide strips running parallel to the hot rolling direction. The 1 inch wide hot rolled strips were subsequently cold rolled from 0.1 inch to a final thickness of 0.0625inch.
notes: A later anneal was mentioned without parameters. Hot-rolling temperatures, sheet quenching and electropolishing solution were not attached to an annealing stage.

source_text: Potentiodynamic Polarization with exposed area of 1 cm2. Potentiodynamic polarization experiments were carried out using a scan rate of 0.1 mV/s commencing at a potential about 250 mV more active than the stable OCP. Before starting the polarization scan, the specimen in the sample holder (WE) was left in the cell for about 1 h to attain a steady state which is shown by a constant potential and current at the beginning of the experiment. The potcntiodynamic runs were programmed such that upon attaining a current density of 25μA/cm^2, the scan direction was reversed and the potentials were scanned back to the starting potential.
notes: About one hour was retained as the reported nominal pre-scan equilibration duration.

Before starting the polarization scan, the specimen in the sample holder (WE) was left in the cell for about 1 h to attain a steady state which is shown by a constant potential and current at the beginning of the experiment. The potcntiodynamic runs were programmed such that upon attaining a current density of 25μA/cm^2, the scan direction was reversed and the potentials were scanned back to the starting potential.
notes: About one hour was retained as the reported nominal pre-scan equilibration duration.

source_text: The stainless steels evaluated in this study were prepared from commercially pure grades of Fe, Ni, ferrochrome, Mn, Mo, Si, manganese or chromium nitride, and chromium carbide. Melting was done in a vacuum induction furnace.The melting procedure consisted of: (1) melting Fe, Ni, Mo, Mn, and ferrochrome in a vacuum; (2) bleeding nitrogen into the furnace; and (3) introducing Mn4N or CrN, wrapped in iron foil, into the melt, as needed. After casting, only solid sections of the ingots were taken to prepare test specimens. The sections were first soaked for 30 minutes and hot rolled. The temperatures were 1205 C and 1095 C, depending upon hot ductility of the heats. The hot rolled specimens were pickled in a solution containing 10% HNO3 and 2% HF at 65 C to remove the hot working scale, cold rolled to 2 mm, annealed at 1065 C for 5 minutes, water quenched, and pickled again in the same HNO3-HF solution at 65 C. A small section was cut from each heat and used for chemical analysis.
notes: The repeated pickling bath was identified as HF + HNO3. Percentage bases and pickling duration were not established. Heating/annealing durations did not become Prep_time, and bath temperature did not become CP_temp.

After casting, only solid sections of the ingots were taken to prepare test specimens. The sections were first soaked for 30 minutes and hot rolled. The temperatures were 1205 C and 1095 C, depending upon hot ductility of the heats. The hot rolled specimens were pickled in a solution containing 10% HNO3 and 2% HF at 65 C to remove the hot working scale, cold rolled to 2 mm, annealed at 1065 C for 5 minutes, water quenched, and pickled again in the same HNO3-HF solution at 65 C. A small section was cut from each heat and used for chemical analysis.
notes: The repeated pickling bath was identified as HF + HNO3. Percentage bases and pickling duration were not established. Heating/annealing durations did not become Prep_time, and bath temperature did not become CP_temp.

source_text: Potentiostatic Polarization. The experimental procedure was to first polarize the electrode potentiostatically at the least noble potential within the passive region for at least 15 min in order to achieve steady-state passivity. The potential was then advanced in stages of 50 mV, allowing 5 min between each change. Initially the current decreased or remained constant after each potential adjustment, but eventually a steadily increasing current at some potential V'c indicated the onset of pitting (or of transpassivity). Steady-state values Vc were obtained subsequently by holding the potential for long times at a fixed value and then observing pitting or the lack of it under a low power microscope. The lowest potential for which pitting could not be observed after a 10-hr or longer period of constant polarization was considered to be the steady-state value Vc. Reproducibility was in the order of ±5 mv.
notes: At least 15 minutes was a lower bound, not an exact preparation duration. Any different earlier pickling time was not substituted for this conditioning duration. Later 5-minute steps and >=10-hour pitting observations were excluded.

source_text: The electrodes were abraded to a final 3/0 emery paper, and pickled usually in 15% HNO3, 5% HF at 80 oC for 5 min to remove the cold worked surface.
notes: The slash emery grade was unconverted. The usual five-minute pickling duration was a nominal protocol, not an exact per-sample measurement; if a separate bounded conditioning step was reported, Prep_time remained unresolved. Percentage bases were not assumed.
A bound or multiple preparation stages prevented a single exact duration; numeric values from another preparation step were not substituted.

source_text: Potentiostatic Polarization. The experimental procedure was to first polarize the electrode potentiostatically at the least noble potential within the passive region for at least 15 min in order to achieve steady-state passivity. The potential was then advanced in stages of 50 mV, allowing 5 min between each change. Initially the current decreased or remained constant after each potential adjustment, but eventually a steadily increasing current at some potential V'c indicated the onset of pitting (or of transpassivity). Steady-state values Vc were obtained subsequently by holding the potential for long times at a fixed value and then observing pitting or the lack of it under a low power microscope. The lowest potential for which pitting could not be observed after a 10-hr or longer period of constant polarization was considered to be the steady-state value Vc. Reproducibility was in the order of ±5 mv.
notes: At least 15 minutes was a lower bound, not an exact preparation duration. Any different earlier pickling time was not substituted for this conditioning duration. Later 5-minute steps and >=10-hour pitting observations were excluded.

source_text: All surfaces of the cast slabs were ground to remove imperfections and provide good rolling surfaces before annealing 16 hours at 1200C in argon atmosphere. The slabs were hot rolled at 1090C to 1/16 inch thickness. Oxide scale was subsequently removed by sand blasting before a final annealing treatment. Following preparation, each alloy was hot rolled to 0.1 inch sheet and water quenched. Hot rolling temperatures were restricted to a maximum of 982C and a minimum of 816C. The hot rolled sheet was electropolished in an aqueous 15wt% NaCl/ 30wt%H2SO4 electrolyte to remove surface scale and sheared into 1 inch wide strips running parallel to the hot rolling direction. The 1 inch wide hot rolled strips were subsequently cold rolled from 0.1 inch to a final thickness of 0.0625inch.
notes: Reported surface operations during processing were retained along with later sample preparation. The electropolishing bath was a preparation mixture, not a test solution. Its mass percentages remained in the original description; no preparation concentration columns were added.

source_text: Potentiodynamic Polarization. The electrodes for the potentiodynamic studies were mounted in epoxy plastic with a single exposed surface parallel to the rolling plane. Electrical contact was made by soft-soldering a nickel wire to the back of the electrode. Contact between the solder or lead wire and the electrolyte was excluded by the plastic and glass tube. The 0.5 by 0.6 cm exposed surface was polished by using standard metallographic techniques, finishing with a distilled water slurry of 0.3 mu alumina. The edges of the electrode were masked with clear Glyptal varnish to prevent crevice corrosion. The coupons for the exposure tests, 2.5 by 2.5 by 0.3 cm, were surface ground and then polished through No. 600 wet silicon carbide paper. They were solvent degreased and rinsed in methanol before exposure.
notes: Only the pitting-test electrode preparation was used. No. 600 paper and solvent/methanol cleaning referred to different exposure-test coupons and were not assigned to the pitting samples. Alumina particle size was not surface roughness or grit.

source_text: Potentiodynamic Polarization - the sample was stabilized in the electrolyte, which was sparged continuously with oxygen (O2), until the potential change was < 1 mV/min, and this potential was considered as the OCP. Then, the sample was scanned potentiodynamically at a rate of 600 mV/h to a potential corresponding to a current density of 10–3 A/cm2 and then scan direction was reversed.
notes: An equilibration criterion was reported, but no duration. Oxygen sparging did not establish a binary agitation value.

source_text: Potentiostatic Polarization. For most of the measurements, Al electrodes were employed measuring 1.5 cm long and 0.4 cm in diameter. One end of each electrode was drilled and tapped, allowing a threaded member attached to a nickel wire to hold the electrode firmly against a glass tube separated by a water-tight Teflon gasket. Only the electrode surface, totally immersed, Teflon, and glass made contact with the electrolyte. Specimens were polished to 3/0 emery paper followed by pickling in 2N NaOH at 80~ for 5 min and then washing in distilled water.
notes: The slash emery grade was left unconverted. The active pickling bath was NaOH, distinct from rinse water and the corrosion-test solution. Its five-minute duration was retained; normality was not converted to molarity.
